Tim king, grieving over the separation from his son, continued 
to describe the infamous deed, the slaying of the young ascetic,

" 0 Kaushalya, having unwittingly committed this impious 
deed, I, deeply distressed, ldlected what could now be done

the pitcher, 1illed with water, I bore it to the ascetic's hermitage

together, like two birds bereft of their wings. Motionless, 
deprived by me of their support, they sat, conversing of their son 
and awaiting the water. My mind was clouded with grief and 
I was smitten with fear, but seeing the aged pair, my anguish 
was increased a thousandfold.

" Beholding the muni, and as one sorely dismayed, I uttered

• 0 Mahatma, I am not thy son, my name is Dasarstha and I 
am a kshattiya. A sinful act has been committed by me of

unknowingly slain by me without design ; what was to happen, 
has been accomplished Thou art a sage, now do what thou 
cnnsiderest proper. • 
" Heating the tale of my evil deed from my own lips, the sage 
reftained from pronouncing a curse on me. His eyes suffused 
with tears and his heart distressed, he addressed me who 
supplicated him with joined palms, saying : • 0 King, if thou 
thyself had'st not coofessed this evil deed to me, thy head had 
instantly split into a thousand pieces by my curse. 0 King, 
the killing of one dwelling in the forest by a kshatriya causes 
him to lose his status, even if he be Indrs. If anyone knowingly 
anacks a sage or spiritual preceptor with a weapon, his head 
is severed into seven pieces. Thou livest still, since the deed 
was done by thee without design, else hadst thou and the whole 
House of Raghu perished.'

AYODHYA KANDA 
" 0 Kaushalya, the sage said : ' Take me to the place where 
the body of my son is lying, I wish to acquaint myself with 
his final state. Alas ! Under the decree of destiny he is lying 
lifeless on the earth. his body besmeared with blood, stripped 
of the deerskin formerly worn by him.' 
" 0 Kaushalya, taking the deeply distressed sage and his wife 
to that place, they, with their fingers touched the lifeless body 
of their son. Approaching the place, they embraced the dead 
body of their child, the father crying : ' 0 Child, thou art to-day 
not bidding us welcome, nor dost thou speak to me. Why art 
thou lyiug on the earth. art thou displeased? 0 My Son, if 
thou art angry with me, regard thy virtuous mother. 
Why 
dost thou not embrace me and speak tender words to me ? 
Now that balf the night has gone, who will read the Scriptures

perform our morning ablutions and after offering up his morning 
devotions, serve and console us? Helpless and destitute, who will 
gather roots, berries and fruits for me in the forest, and feed me, 
like a beloved guest ? 0 My Son, how shall I nourish and 
support thy mother, blind, ascetic and devoted to her son? 
0 My Child, stay, stay, do not yet enter the abode of Yama. 
To-morrowthymotherandlwill accompany thee. Without thee

pany thee to the abode ofYama. Beholding the Lord of Death,

which have caused us to be separated from our son and let 
him yet be our support. Grant us this blessing, 0 Lord of

state attained by those who follow truth and suffer death at the

" Thus for a long time wsiling in distress, the aged parents 
began to offer ceremonial water for their dead son. The son 
of that sage by virtue of his meritorious deeds ascending to

I shall fed no grief in dying. This was my only son and by 
slaying him thou hast rendered me childless. As he was slain 
by thee, I pronounce a curse on thee. Mayest thou suffer the 
the same grief that thou hast caused to me, through separation 
from thy son, ending in thy death. 0 King, having slain the 
sage unknowingly, the guilt of killing a brahmin will not be 
thine. As the dispenser of charity receives the merit of those

caused me, putting an end to thy life.' 
" 0 Queen, having cursed me, they lamented for some time 
and then gathering wood, kindled a fire, and entering it, departed 
this life. 0 Lady, to-day recalling that evil deed, committed 
thoughtlessly in my youth, by discharging the arrow by sound, 
the fruit of my action has overtaken me, as illness follows the 
partaking of unwholesome food. 0 Noble Lady, the time of 
the fullilment of the sage's cnrse has come." 
Having said this, the king weeping and overcome with fear 
on the approach of death, spoke again : " 0 Kaushalya, I am

0 Kauahalya, 0 V'lttUODI Snmitra, I depart ! 0 My Cruel

brief.summary_1line: King Dasharatha recounts accidentally killing a hermit’s son, recalls the curse of dying from grief for his own son, and finally dies mourning Rama’s exile.

image_candidates.scene_text: The blind hermit parents kneel in the forest, embracing the blood-stained body of their dead son while King Dasharatha stands nearby in grief.
The young ascetic’s spirit rises in a celestial form beside Indra’s chariot, speaking to his mourning parents on the forest floor.
King Dasharatha lies on his bed in the palace at midnight, reaching out blindly while crying for Rama as the queens Kaushalya and Sumitra mourn beside him.

deep.rich_summary: King Dasaratha, broken by Rama’s exile, confesses to Queen Kaushalya the youthful sin that now returns as fate. While hunting by sound at the Sarayu river, he once mistook the filling of a water pot for an animal and shot an arrow, mortally wounding a young ascetic who had been gathering water for his blind parents. Dasaratha carried the water to the hermitage and revealed the tragedy. The grieving parents mourned over their son’s body; the son briefly appeared in a celestial form and ascended to heaven. Before dying, the father cursed the king: he too would die from grief caused by separation from his son. Remembering this curse as Rama remains in exile, Dasaratha realizes destiny has arrived. Overwhelmed by remorse and longing to see Rama once more, he laments bitterly and finally dies in the night.

highlight_spans.why: The chapter opening situates the episode within the Ayodhya Kanda, framing the tragic confession that explains Dasaratha’s fate.
Dasaratha’s confession describing how he mistakenly shot the ascetic while hunting by sound—the pivotal action that drives the curse and the king’s eventual death.
The blind father’s anguished lament over his dead son, one of the most emotionally powerful passages in the episode.
The dead ascetic’s ascent to heaven in a celestial form and aerial chariot introduces a brief divine revelation amid the tragedy.
Dasaratha’s final lament for Rama and his realization that the sage’s curse has come true, culminating in his death from grief.

top_scenes.scene_text: The dying young ascetic rises in a radiant celestial form beside Indra and ascends into the sky in a shining aerial chariot while his grieving parents watch below.
The blind ascetic parents kneel in the forest, embracing the blood‑stained body of their son as King Dasaratha stands nearby in horror and remorse.
Inside the dark palace chamber at midnight, the aged King Dasaratha lies collapsing in grief, calling out Rama’s name as Kaushalya and Sumitra stand beside him.
